summary: This document specifies the GNU Name System (GNS), a decentralized, censorship-resistant name resolution protocol that offers a privacy-enhancing alternative to DNS. It defines the wire format, resolution process, cryptography, and security and privacy considerations. It was developed outside the IETF and does not have IETF consensus.

eli5.summary: Usually one big phone book tells you where names live. GNS is a way for everyone to keep their own pages, so no single person can erase a name.

questions: what is the gnu name system
how does key blinding work in gns
subtitle: Decentralized, censorship-resistant DNS alternative using key blinding and cryptographic zone management.

tldr.problem: DNS is centralized: root servers control top-level domains, and DNS queries are often unencrypted and observable. Users have no way to operate their own globally unique namespace or prevent domain seizure and censorship at the protocol level.
tldr.mechanism: GNS (GNU Name System) is a petname system where users manage their own zones (similar to DNS zones) identified by cryptographic zone keys. Zone contents are encrypted and stored in distributed hash tables. Names are resolved recursively using key blinding (ZKDF) to derive distinct lookup keys from zone keys and labels, preventing zone enumeration. Each resource record is signed with a derived key, allowing signature verification without revealing the zone key.
tldr.outcome: Users can create and publish their own domains, control them cryptographically, and resolve names with privacy (lookups do not reveal zone structure). The system operates without a central authority and can use any distributed storage; it does not expect all users to share a common root zone.

facts.label: PoW algorithm
facts.value: Argon2id with 3 iterations, 1024 KiB memory, 64-byte output

facts.label: Zone key
facts.value: 256-bit public key (wire format depends on zone type)

facts.label: Label encoding
facts.value: UTF-8 in Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC)

today: RFC 9498 is an Informational RFC from the IETF Independent Submissions Editor, published in November 2023. It specifies the GNS protocol as developed outside the IETF by the GNUnet community. The protocol has existing implementations in GNUnet and is not on the standards track.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Principles
sections.content:
The GNU Name System (GNS) is a decentralized, censorship-resistant, and privacy-preserving domain name resolution protocol. Unlike DNS, GNS does not assume all users share the same root zone or trust a central authority. Instead, it follows a petname system model: users assign local memorable names to cryptographic zone identities. Zones are uniquely identified by their zone key and zone type, and users can configure their own Start Zones (the initial zones to consult during resolution).

GNS provides three key properties: First, global names through zTLDs: a zone key is statistically unique, so a zone top-level domain (zTLD)—an encoding of the zone key—is globally unique. Names ending with a zTLD are globally unique but not memorable. Second, memorable petnames for zones: users configure local, memorable names (petnames) that map to zone keys, providing convenient, non-global references. Third, secure mappings from names to records: zone owners map labels to resource records or delegations to other zones. These mappings are cryptographically signed and encrypted before publication.

This specification defines the wire format of resource records, resolution processes, cryptographic routines, and security considerations. It was developed outside the IETF and does not have IETF consensus; it is published to guide implementations and ensure interoperability.
sections.eli5: GNS lets each person run their own domain name system. Your favorite zone gets a personal nickname, your records are locked and signed, and nobody can spy on what you're looking up or tell you that a name doesn't exist when it does.

sections.title: Zones and Name Resolution
sections.content:
A zone in GNS is uniquely identified by its zone key (usually a public key) and zone type. A zone contains resource records that map labels to information. A label is a UTF-8 string; labels in a name are separated by dots. Zone ownership is determined by possession of the private key corresponding to the zone key.

Name resolution begins at a configured Start Zone and follows zone delegations recursively. For each label in a name, a resolver fetches the corresponding record set from distributed storage (typically a DHT). The critical innovation is key blinding: a zone key derivation function (ZKDF) blinds the zone key using the label to produce a blinded zone key that is statistically unlinkable to the original zone key and to other blinded keys derived from different labels. This prevents zone enumeration: without knowledge of both the zone key and the label, an attacker cannot determine which encrypted record sets belong to a zone.

Records are signed using the private key derived from the blinded zone key, and signatures are verified against the blinded public key. This allows resolution to proceed with signature verification without ever disclosing the zone key itself to remote storage.
sections.eli5: Each person's zone is like a locked box. To find a record for label 'alice', you derive a special key just for 'alice' without revealing what zone you're looking in. You check the signature on the record without knowing the master key.

sections.title: Record Types and Storage
sections.content:
GNS defines several record types for different purposes. Zone delegation records (PKEY and EDKEY) are used to delegate subdomains to other zones; they include the zone type and zone key of the delegated zone. Redirection records (REDIRECT and GNS2DNS) allow a label to point to another label within the zone (REDIRECT) or to delegate to DNS (GNS2DNS). Auxiliary records support operations and DNS compatibility: LEHO provides a DNS-compatible label hint, NICK suggests a petname for the zone, and BOX allows boxed records (records that do not cause delegation).

Zone contents are published to distributed storage using deterministic encryption (to enable caching). Before publishing, plaintext records are encrypted using a key derived from the zone key, label, and expiration timestamp. The encrypted data is then signed using the derived private key. The resulting ciphertext and signature are stored at a location derived from the blinded zone key.
sections.eli5: GNS records come in types: some point to other zones, some point to other records, and some contain data. Each one is encrypted and signed so only the right people can read and verify it.

sections.title: Cryptographic Operations and Zone Revocation
sections.content:
Each zone type defines a complete set of cryptographic functions: key generation, zone key derivation (ZKDF), symmetric encryption/decryption, signing, and verification. The RFC specifies two default zone types using ECDSA with SHA-512 for signing and AES-256 for encryption. Future zone types can introduce new cipher suites for cryptographic agility.

To revoke a zone, the owner publishes a signed revocation message along with a proof of work (PoW). The PoW uses Argon2id with fixed parameters to prevent flooding attacks. A revocation message includes 32 unique PoW values, each with at least 22 leading zero bits on average, along with a timestamp and the zone key. Implementers must verify the signature, check for duplicate PoWs, and confirm that the average difficulty is sufficient. Revocations are broadcasted through the network and stored locally; once validated, they must be considered during delegation record processing (preventing resolution through a revoked zone).
sections.eli5: To sign things, you use your private key. To revoke your zone (cancel all its records), you prove you've done some hard computational work so people know you really meant it and aren't just flooding the network.

sections.title: Security, Privacy, and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Availability: GNS relies on distributed storage; availability depends on the underlying DHT or storage system. Unlike DNS with its centralized root, GNS has no single point of failure for global operation, but individual zones depend on their publishers to maintain replicas.

Zone privacy: Key blinding prevents an observer from learning which records belong to a zone without knowing the zone key and labels. However, if a label is public knowledge, an observer can link all queries for that label to a single zone.

Namespace ambiguity: A GNS name is indistinguishable from a DNS name. Users and applications must be careful to avoid confusion (for example, 'example.gns.alt' vs. 'example.com'). The RFC recommends applications use the '.gns.alt' suffix for GNS domains to signal intent.

Zone governance: Zone owners must manage their private keys carefully. Loss of the private key means permanent loss of the zone. Circular delegations (a zone delegating a subdomain to itself or to a zone that delegates back) are explicitly allowed and can be used for alias-like behavior.
sections.eli5: GNS is as available as the computers storing it. Your name is private if your labels stay secret. Don't mix GNS names with DNS names or people will get confused. Guard your zone key or lose your domain forever.
